problem: Deep RL navigation from raw images needs huge amounts of experience (millions of episodes, extra feedback like velocity or reward), which is impractical for real robots. Existing real-image navigation environments such as StreetLearn have limited appearance diversity, with a single dataset and no day/night or seasonal changes.
motivation: Real-world navigation needs both visual place recognition and self-motion/goal feedback, and robots need sample-efficient policies that generalize across extreme appearance changes. Place-recognition features are compact and appearance-robust, so they may replace raw pixels as RL input, but no benchmark existed to test this on city-scale, multi-traversal data.
key_idea: Encode images with off-the-shelf VPR/deep models (NetVLAD, ResNet-50) into compact features, concatenate them with a 1-d goal signal into a bimodal representation, and train a PPO+LSTM policy on a single traversal in the new CityLearn Unity environment built from real-world datasets.
insight: Smaller (64-d) representations gave better generalization and sample efficiency for RL, even though larger features give better VPR AUC. Training time dropped from 29h48m (raw images) to 11m (about 2 orders of magnitude). The raw-image agent failed under day-to-night change while NetVLAD 64-d completed the task (deployment comparison).
method: CityLearn environment: Unity/ML-Agents framework that loads real-world datasets (10+ datasets, 100+ traversals, 60+ cities, e.g. Oxford RobotCar, Nordland, KITTI, BDD) as interactive navigation environments with appearance and viewpoint changes, small average step (0.05 m) and 2GB RAM per environment.
Visual encoders: off-the-shelf NetVLAD (VGG-16, PCA+whitening) at 4096/2048/512/64-d and ImageNet ResNet-50 (2048-d, reduced to 512/64-d with NetVLAD's dimensionality reduction).
Bimodal representation: visual feature x_t concatenated with a 1-d goal destination g_t, giving 65/513/2049/4097-d vectors.
Policy network: 512-unit MLP encoding b_t, combined with previous action a_{t-1} into a 256-unit LSTM, with policy and value heads, trained with PPO using 16 concurrent agents.
Reward and curriculum: sparse +1 on reaching target, -1/ms penalty when heading away from the goal, 7 curriculum levels of increasingly distant destinations.
Baselines: a 'baseline' agent using 1-d position instead of images (100% completion), and a 'raw images' agent with a 2-layer CNN on 84x84 RGB trained end-to-end.
Evaluation: VPR AUC using an MLP classifier per reference traversal; navigation completed/failed percentage on the training traversal and on query traversals with extreme changes.

setting.backbone: NetVLAD (VGG-16, frozen, pretrained) / ResNet-50 (ImageNet, frozen) features + MLP-LSTM PPO policy trained from scratch
setting.model_size: policy: 512-unit MLP + 256-unit LSTM (small); encoders VGG-16 / ResNet-50
setting.training_data: RL on a single traversal (Nordland summer or Oxford RobotCar day); encoders pretrained off-the-shelf; no extra data
setting.observation: monocular RGB encoded into 64-4096-d features plus 1-d goal signal and previous action
setting.simulator: CityLearn (Unity ML-Agents) built on real datasets (Oxford RobotCar, Nordland)
setting.privileged: 1-d goal destination signal provided; no map

numbers_note: No tabulated navigation metrics; results appear only in figures (RL curves, completed/failed statistics, AUC) and a few text values (average reward 92% NetVLAD-64, 80% ResNet-50-64, 99% baseline; training time 29h48m to 11m). Not a standard benchmark, so no entries.
results: With 64-d NetVLAD or ResNet-50 features, the policy reaches average reward of 92% and 80% versus 99% for the position-based baseline. It trains about 2 orders of magnitude faster than the raw-image agent (29h48m to 11m) and generalizes across day-to-night (Oxford RobotCar) and summer-to-winter (Nordland), where the raw-image agent fails.
limitations: Evaluation is on only two datasets, with a 1-d goal signal and a discrete traversal-following setup, so it is far from full free-space navigation.
Results are given mostly in figures with no numeric table; no comparison to other published navigation methods.
Single-frame VPR features only, with no multi-frame temporal matching and no real-robot deployment.
